What the Market is Pricing In

Texas Instruments is trading at $284.65, which corresponds to an elevated 36.5x normalized Price to Owner Earnings and 37.2x Enterprise Value to Owner Earnings. This premium pricing reflects aggressive market enthusiasm following the recent beat-and-raise quarterly results, wherein reported revenue rebounded 27.8% year over year to $6.06 billion, alongside confirmation that trailing twelve-month free cash flow inflected to $8.4 billion as multi-year 300mm fab capital expenditures tapered from $4.8 billion down to $2.6 billion. Investors are enthusiastically extrapolating this cyclical recovery, bidding up TXN under the belief that secular content expansion in automotive electrification and AI data center power management, combined with a structural 40% unpackaged die cost advantage from captive 300mm manufacturing, permanently insulates the business from historical downcycles.

However, Mr. Market's euphoric pricing creates an asymmetric risk profile. Skeptics note that trading at 36.5x normalized owner earnings assumes cyclical peak operating margins of nearly 47% and mid-60s gross margins can be sustained indefinitely without macro interruption. The market is pricing current channel replenishment as durable structural expansion, largely ignoring the risk that current unit shipments represent a transitory inventory snapback after an eight-quarter destocking drought. In essence, today's price implies that TXN will maintain high single-digit revenue compounding while operating at peak mid-cycle cash conversion, leaving zero margin of safety for macroeconomic deceleration or mounting mature-node analog competition.

2
Forensic Business Headwinds
Skeptics identify three critical structural vulnerabilities. First, recent demand acceleration has been amplified by aggressive channel restocking and rolling price hikes across catalog parts, which risks driving customer pushback. Second, heavily subsidized domestic Chinese analog competitors (such as SG Micro and 3Peak) are aggressively qualifying pin-to-pin compatible power management and signal chain alternatives, threatening TI's exposure to Asian electronics assembly supply chains. Third, as massive 300mm cleanroom complexes in Sherman and Lehi transition from construction-in-progress into active commercial service, fixed straight-line depreciation charges will hit cost of goods sold, triggering negative operating leverage if factory utilization drops.
3
Skeptic Unit Contraction
If customer restocking runs out of steam and Asian substitution takes hold, shipment volumes of catalog analog and embedded processing ICs contract by 8.0% over three years, while competitive discounting compresses net average selling prices by 3.0%. Consequently, annualized revenue deteriorates from the current $24,220.0M run-rate down to $21,614.0M by Year 3.
4
Reverse Operating Leverage & Cash Degradation
Because semiconductor fabrication entails rigid fixed overhead, cash manufacturing costs, R&D, and SG&A cannot be scaled down proportionally. Against $21,614.0M in degraded Year 3 revenue, cash cost of goods sold consumes $9,200.0M, cash operating expenses consume $3,450.0M, cash taxes consume $927.0M, ongoing maintenance CapEx absorbs $1,250.0M, and stock-based compensation consumes $340.0M. This leaves degraded Year 3 Owner Earnings of $6,447.0M ($7.00/share on 921.0M shares).
5
Downside Risk Valuation Floor
In a cyclical downturn where earnings contract and return on invested capital compresses, the market historically derates mature analog semiconductors toward conservative valuation multiples. Capitalizing degraded Year 3 Owner Earnings of $7.00/share at a conservative 22.0x P/OE trough multiple yields $154.00/share, which when combined with an estimated ending net cash position of -$4.00/share (reflecting modest net debt reduction from residual operating cash flow after dividends), produces a Downside Floor Target of $150.00/share.

How Things Are Going Now

Operationally, Texas Instruments is executing through a powerful cyclical inflection across its core Analog and Embedded Processing units through full-year 2025 and heading into 2026 results. Across the four quarters of 2025 leading into early 2026, revenue inflected sequentially from $4,423.0M to $4,825.0M, $5,463.0M, and $6,055.0M in the final quarter of 2025 (up 27.8% year over year), establishing a current annualized revenue run-rate of $24,220.0M entering 2026. Top-line expansion has been led by the Analog division, which surged 32.0% year over year to $4,911.0M, supported by broad replenishment in industrial automation, expanding battery management and ADAS content in automotive tiers, and strong demand for high-efficiency power management integrated circuits across high-density AI data center clusters. Embedded Processing also demonstrated solid traction, expanding 21.0% year over year to $858.0M.

Profitability metrics have advanced in tandem with factory loading through 2025 and into 2026. Across 2025 reported results, gross margin steadily expanded from 55.9% to 58.0%, 61.4%, and 64.2%, while operating margin expanded from 33.3% to 47.4% ($2,870.0M in operating profit). This performance underscores the unit-cost leverage unlocked by the commercial ramp of 300mm wafer fabs in Richardson and Lehi exiting 2025, which deliver approximately 40% lower unpackaged die costs compared to standard 200mm facilities. Free cash flow on a trailing twelve-month basis inflected upward to $8.4 billion in 2025, directly driven by the moderation of capital expenditures down to $2.6 billion from peak multi-year outlays near $4.8 billion.

Capital allocation remains shareholder-oriented entering 2026. Management declared its 23rd consecutive annual dividend increase in late 2025, raising the quarterly dividend 7.0% to $1.52 per share ($6.08 annualized), while continuing modest opportunistic share repurchases. The balance sheet carries $8,142.0M in liquid cash and short-term investments against $12,905.0M in debt, representing a net debt position of -$4,763M (-$5.17/share).
